'''László Lovász''' ({{IPA|hu|ˈlovaːs ˈlaːsloː |lang}}; born March 9, 1948) is a Hungarian mathematician and professor emeritus at [[Eötvös Loránd University]], best known for his work in [[combinatorics]], for which he was awarded the 2021 [[Abel Prize]] jointly with [[Avi Wigderson]]. He was the president of the [[International Mathematical Union]] from 2007 to 2010 and the president of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] from 2014 to 2020.

In [[graph theory]], Lovász's notable contributions include the proofs of [[Kneser's conjecture]] and the [[Lovász local lemma]], as well as the formulation of the [[Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture]]. He is also one of the eponymous authors of the [[Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice basis reduction algorithm|LLL lattice reduction algorithm]].

==Early life and education==
Lovász was born on March 9, 1948, in [[Budapest]], Hungary.<ref name="NYT-Abel"/><ref name="Quanta-Abel"/><ref name="CV"/>

Lovász attended the [[Fazekas Mihály Gimnázium (Budapest)|Fazekas Mihály Gimnázium]] in Budapest.<ref name="60th">{{cite book |title=Building Bridges |chapter=Preface |editor1-first= Martin |editor1-last=Grötschel |editor1-link=Martin Grötschel |editor2-first=Gyula O. H. |editor2-last=Katona |editor2-link=Gyula O. H. Katona |publisher=[[János Bolyai Mathematical Society]] and [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2008 |pages=7–8}}</ref> He won three gold medals (1964–1966) and one silver medal (1963) at the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]].<ref name="NYT-Abel"/><ref name="Quanta-Abel"/><ref>{{IMO results |id=9852}}</ref><ref name="60th"/> He also participated in a Hungarian game show about math prodigies.<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/> [[Paul Erdős]] helped introduce Lovász to [[graph theory]] at a young age.<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/><ref name="Nature"/>

Lovász received his [[Candidate of Sciences]] (C.Sc.) degree in 1970 at the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/><ref name="Fields"/><ref name="CV"/>  His advisor was [[Tibor Gallai]].<ref name="Fields">{{cite web|title=László Lovász, Director, Institute of Mathematics, Eötvös Loránd University Budapest, Hungary|url=https://www.fields.utoronto.ca/programs/scientific/07-08/public_lectures/lovasz.html|publisher=fields|date=February 11, 2008|access-date=December 4, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=15779}}</ref> He received his first doctorate ([[Dr. rer. nat.|Dr.Rer.Nat.]]) degree from [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in 1971 and his second doctorate (Dr.Math.Sci.) from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1977.<ref name="CV"/>

==Career==
From 1971 to 1975, Lovász worked at Eötvös Loránd University as a research associate.<ref name="CV"/> From 1975 to 1978, he was a [[Docent#Central and Eastern Europe|docent]] at the [[University of Szeged]], and then served as a professor and the Chair of Geometry there until 1982.<ref name="CV"/> He then returned to Eötvös Loránd University as a professor and the Chair of Computer Science until 1993.<ref name="CV"/>

Lovász was a professor at [[Yale University]] from 1993 to 1999, when he moved to the [[Microsoft Research Center]] where he worked as a senior researcher until 2006.<ref name="CV"/> He returned to [[Eötvös Loránd University]] where he was the director of the Mathematical Institute (2006–2011)<ref>{{cite web|title=LOVÁSZ, László|url=http://www.sciforum.hu/programme/speakers-and-abstracts/lovasz-laszlo.html|publisher=World Science Forum|access-date=December 4, 2019}}</ref> and a professor in the Department of Computer Science (2006–2018).<ref name="CV">{{cite web |url=https://web.cs.elte.hu/~lovasz/vita.pdf |title=Curriculum Vitae |website=László Lovász |access-date=March 17, 2021}}</ref> He retired in 2018.<ref name="CV"/>

Lovász was the president of the [[International Mathematical Union]] between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2010.<ref>[http://www.mathunion.org/Organization/EC/2007-2010.html The IMU Executive Committee 2007–2010] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071229013327/http://www.mathunion.org/Organization/EC/2007-2010.html |date=December 29, 2007 }}</ref><ref name="Nature"/> In 2014, he was elected the president of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] (MTA) and served until 2020.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20140512064619/http://mta.hu/mta_hirei/lovasz_laszlo-a-magyar-tudomanyos-akademia-uj-elnoke-134141// Magyar Tudományos Akadémia: "Lovász László a Magyar Tudományos Akadémia új elnöke", 2014/05/06] (in Hungarian)</ref><ref>[https://mta.hu/mta_hirei/a-lekoszono-es-az-uj-elnok-beszedevel-zarult-az-mta-193-kozgyulese-110730// Magyar Tudományos Akadémia: "A leköszönő és az új elnök beszédével zárult az MTA 193. közgyűlése", 2020/07/09] (in Hungarian)</ref><ref name="Nature"/>

==Research==
In collaboration with Erdős in the 1970s, Lovász developed complementary methods to Erdős's existing [[probabilistic graph theory]] techniques.<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/> This included the [[Lovász local lemma]], which has become a standard technique for [[existence theorem|proving the existence]] of rare [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]s.<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/> Also in graph theory, Lovász proved [[Kneser's conjecture]] and helped formulate the [[Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture]].<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/>

With [[Arjen Lenstra]] and [[Hendrik Lenstra]] in 1982, Lovász developed the [[Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice basis reduction algorithm|LLL algorithm]] for approximating points in [[Lattice (group)|lattices]] and [[lattice reduction|reducing their bases]].<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lenstra|first1=A. K.|author1-link=A. K. Lenstra|last2=Lenstra|first2=H. W. Jr. |author2-link=H. W. Lenstra, Jr.|last3=Lovász|first3=L.|author3-link=László Lovász|title=Factoring polynomials with rational coefficients|journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]]|volume=261|year=1982|issue=4|pages=515–534|hdl=1887/3810|doi=10.1007/BF01457454|mr=0682664|citeseerx=10.1.1.310.318|s2cid=5701340}}</ref> The LLL algorithm has been described by [[Gil Kalai]] as "one of the fundamental algorithms" and has been used in several practical applications, including [[Factorization of polynomials|polynomial factorization]] algorithms and [[cryptography]].<ref name="Quanta-Abel"/>

[[Donald Knuth]] named Lovász as one of his combinatorial heroes in a 2023 interview.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Bhāvanā: The mathematics magazine|url=https://bhavana.org.in/the-dawn-of-rigour-in-the-art-of-programming/|title=The dawn of rigour in the art of programming|type=Interview with Donald Knuth|first1=Sudhir|last1=Rao|first2=Indranath|last2=Sengupta|volume=7|issue=1|date=January 2023|access-date=2024-02-04}}</ref>

==Awards==
Lovász was awarded the [[Pólya Prize (SIAM)|Pólya Prize]] in 1979, the [[Fulkerson Prize]] in 1982 and 2012, the [[Brouwer Medal]] in 1993, the [[Wolf Prize]] and [[Knuth Prize]] in 1999, the [[Gödel Prize]] in 2001, the [[John von Neumann Theory Prize]] in 2006, the {{ill|János Bolyai Creative Prize|hu|Bolyai János alkotói díj}} in 2007, the [[Széchenyi Prize]] in 2008, and the [[Kyoto Prize in Basic Sciences]] in 2010.<ref name="CV"/><ref name="Notices-2010">{{cite journal |title=Lovász Receives Kyoto Prize |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=57 |issue=9 |year=2010 |page=1136 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201009/rtx100901136p.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.informs.org/Recognizing-Excellence/Award-Recipients/Laszlo-Lovasz |title=László Lovász |website=[[Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences]] |access-date=March 17, 2021}}</ref> In March 2021, he shared the [[Abel Prize]] with [[Avi Wigderson]] from the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] "for their foundational contributions to [[theoretical computer science]] and [[discrete mathematics]], and their leading role in shaping them into central fields of modern mathematics".<ref name="NYT-Abel">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/17/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html|title=2 Win Abel Prize for Work That Bridged Math and Computer Science|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|first=Kenneth|last=Chang|date=March 17, 2021|access-date=March 17, 2021}}</ref><ref name="Quanta-Abel">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/avi-wigderson-and-laszlo-lovasz-win-abel-prize-20210317/ |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |title=Pioneers Linking Math and Computer Science Win the Abel Prize |first=Kevin |last=Hartnett |date=March 17, 2021 |access-date=March 17, 2021}}</ref><ref name="Nature">{{Cite news|last=Castelvecchi|first=Davide|date=March 17, 2021|title=Abel Prize celebrates union of mathematics and computer science|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-021-00694-9|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|language=en|doi=10.1038/d41586-021-00694-9}}</ref> In 2017 he received [[John von Neumann Professor]] title from the [[Budapest University of Technology and Economics]] (BME) and the [[John von Neumann Computer Society]].<ref name="John von Neumann Professor">Recipients are listed on Budapest University of Technology and Economics website: {{cite web |url=https://www.bme.hu/John-von-Neumann-Professors |title=John von Neumann Professors |publisher=[[Budapest University of Technology and Economics]] |access-date=September 13, 2022}}</ref> In 2021, he received Hungary's highest order, the [[Hungarian Order of Saint Stephen]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://24.hu/tudomany/2021/08/20/az-mta-ket-volt-elnokee-a-szent-istvan-rend/|title=Az MTA két volt elnökéé a Szent István Rend|work=24.hu|date=August 20, 2021|access-date=August 20, 2021|language=hu}}</ref>

He was elected a foreign member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2006<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/foreign-members/7176 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160208205716/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/foreign-members/7176 |title=L. Lovász |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |archive-date=February 8, 2016 |access-date=February 8, 2016}}</ref> and the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in 2007,  and an honorary member of the [[London Mathematical Society]] in 2009.<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120904190513/http://www.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/384/384_01.html%234|title=LMS homepage}}</ref> Lovász was elected as a member of the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Laszlo Lovasz|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/laszlo-lovasz-lubwfu/|access-date=March 22, 2021|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved February 2, 2013.</ref>

==Personal life==
Lovász is married to fellow mathematician [[Katalin Vesztergombi]],<ref>{{citation|language=hu|url=http://nol.hu/kultura/20130712-edes_teher__zseni_az_apam-1399403|title=Édes teher: zseni az apám (interview with László Lovász)|magazine=NOL|date=July 12, 2013 |last1=Zoltán |first1=Ötvös }}</ref> with whom he participated in a program for high school students gifted in mathematics,<ref>{{citation|title=Teaching Gifted Learners in STEM Subjects: Developing Talent in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics|series=Routledge Research in Achievement and Gifted Education|editor1-first=Keith S.|editor1-last=Taber|editor2-first=Manabu|editor2-last=Sumida|editor3-first=Lynne|editor3-last=McClure|publisher=Routledge|year=2017|isbn=978-1-317-44896-9|pages=92–93|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WAgqDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA92}}</ref> and has four children.<ref>{{citation|title=50th IMO - 50 Years of International Mathematical Olympiads|series=|editor1-first=Hans-Dietrich|editor1-last=Gronau|editor2-first= Hanns-Heinrich|editor2-last=Langmann|editor3-first=Dierk|editor3-last=Schleicher|publisher=Springer|year=2011|isbn=978-3-642-14565-0|pages=185|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eEErpZb78vAC&pg=PA185}}</ref><ref name="CV"/> He is a dual citizen of Hungary and the United States.<ref name="CV"/>
